slides.title: Which claims need an experiment
slides.text: Session 1 Which claims need an experiment Explain what random assignment removes from a comparison Classify a study as a randomised experiment, a quasi-experiment or an observational comparison State the causal claim a study supports and the assumption it rests on 01

slides.title: "It works" is a claim about what would have happened without it
slides.text: The word on every report "It works" is a claim about what would have happened without it Sahar Al-Wuhaibi directs Mashraq Municipal Permits Office. Six studies on her desk end with "works". "Works" means: holders did better than they would have done without the change. Nobody can observe one holder with and without a reminder, so every study compares two groups. The question is how the groups came to differ. The case of this course A fictional city permits office. Three changes wait for a decision: a renewal reminder, a redesigned online form, a new routine at the counters of 24 branches. You are Juri Al-Asmari, junior analyst. All data are synthetic.

slides.title: Groups that chose differ in more than the thing they chose
slides.text: Lab 1.1, step 4 Groups that chose differ in more than the thing they chose +3.0 points: the true effect of the app on on-time renewal, set by us in a simulated world +17.0 points: the gap between app users and the others when holders choose +2.5 points: the gap when a coin decides who gets the app Organised holders install the app more often and renew on time more often, app or no app. The volunteer gap measures mostly that hidden trait. Statisticians call it confounding.

slides.title: A coin makes the two groups alike in everything, seen and unseen
slides.text: Random assignment A coin makes the two groups alike in everything, seen and unseen 1 · One pool every holder due a notice in the window → 2 · A seeded coin per holder, not per clerk, branch or weekday → 3 · Two arms the same mix of organised and disorganised, old and new, apart from chance → 4 · One difference the change itself; what remains is sampling error, which has a size The coin does not know who is organised. That is the whole point: it cannot favour a trait nobody measured.

slides.title: More data cure noise. They do not cure bias
slides.text: Lab 1.1, step 4, repeated 200 times More data cure noise. They do not cure bias Comparison Mean gap over 200 repetitions Smallest Largest True effect Holders choose +18.1 points +16.0 +20.2 +3.0 A coin decides +3.0 points +1.0 +4.8 Bias All 200 volunteer comparisons agree with each other, and all are wrong by about 15 points. A larger survey would be wrong more precisely. Noise The coin comparisons scatter around the truth. Day 2 chooses a sample size that makes the scatter small enough.

slides.title: Three designs support three different claims
slides.text: The vocabulary of the first outcome Three designs support three different claims Design How the groups came to differ Claim it supports Example at Mashraq Randomised experiment Chance alone The change caused the difference, for the units in the test A seeded coin per holder; a slot lottery Quasi-experiment A rule or a date nobody chose for themselves Caused, if a stated assumption holds A fee that starts at 10 square metres; booking switched on in six branches Observational comparison People or managers chose The groups differ; the study cannot say why App users against the others; volunteer branches The assignment makes the design, not the intention. A lottery run for fairness is still an experiment.

slides.title: A quasi-experiment is as strong as the assumption you can defend
slides.text: Reading a quasi-experiment A quasi-experiment is as strong as the assumption you can defend The fee line at 10 square metres Stalls of 9.9 and 10.0 square metres are alike, so the gap in renewal is the fee. If nothing else changes at the line, and if holders cannot pick their side of it. Online booking in six branches Compare the change in missed appointments there with the change elsewhere. If both groups would have moved in parallel without it. What goes wrong. The assumption is left unsaid and the result is reported as if a coin had been tossed. Ask for the sentence that starts with "if".

slides.title: Some questions should not be answered with an experiment
slides.text: Before you propose a test Some questions should not be answered with an experiment The benefit is already known. Withholding something proven from half of the citizens is not acceptable. No decision depends on it. If the office will adopt the change whatever the result, do not test it. There are too few units. Three regions cannot be randomised into anything a test can read. The harm cannot be undone. A test needs a guardrail that can stop it in time. At Mashraq every design answers four questions. Who is in each arm? Why is withholding acceptable? Which data are used? Which guardrail stops the test if a group is harmed?

slides.title: Which study lets the office say "caused"?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which study lets the office say "caused"? Mansour Al-Khelaiwi wants to know whether evening opening shortens waits. Four studies are possible. Which one supports "evening opening caused shorter waits" without a further assumption? Compare the branches whose managers asked for evening opening with the rest Draw 12 of the 24 branches by a recorded lottery for evening opening and compare with the other 12 Open all branches in the evening from June and compare waits before and after Compare the waits of evening visitors with those of daytime visitors

slides.title: Six studies, three designs
slides.text: Lab 1.1 · 25 min Six studies, three designs Classify six studies from public services by design and by the causal claim each supports, mark the sheet, then simulate a comparison of volunteers beside a randomised one. D1_1_six_studies.ipynb Read the six studies and name each design 7 min Name the claim each one supports 6 min Mark the sheet against the key 3 min Simulate volunteers beside a coin 6 min Write the claim the app survey supports 3 min ✱ Stretch: Make the hidden trait stronger and watch which of the two gaps moves

slides.title: Decision, hypothesis and metrics
slides.text: Session 2 Decision, hypothesis and metrics Write the decision an experiment informs, with the action for each result Choose one primary metric and set a minimum effect of interest from costs Write guardrails with thresholds and a stop rule that protects holders 02

slides.title: Start from the decision the result will change
slides.text: Where a design starts Start from the decision the result will change 1 · Decision who decides, and what they do for each result → 2 · Hypothesis the change, the metric, the direction → 3 · Metrics one primary, guardrails, a minimum effect → 4 · Stop rule when the test ends and what may end it sooner Sahar's question. "Would a reminder seven days before a permit expires get more holders to renew on time?" Today a holder gets one notice, 30 days before expiry, and nothing after it.

slides.title: The estimand says exactly which number the test estimates
slides.text: One number in a named population The estimand says exactly which number the test estimates Hypothesis: holders who get the reminder renew on time more often than holders who get only the standard notice. Estimand: the difference in the share renewing on time, reminder minus control, among holders sent a notice in the test window. It names the metric, the two arms, the direction of the subtraction and the population. What it leaves out on purpose Other permit offices. Other seasons. Holders who got no notice in the window. The result will be about the holders in the test; everything else is an argument you make afterwards, in words.

slides.title: One metric carries the decision; the others explain or protect
slides.text: Three jobs One metric carries the decision; the others explain or protect Kind Its job In the reminder test Primary Decides. Exactly one, defined with its time window. On-time renewal: renewed on or before the expiry date. Baseline 61.6%. Secondary Explains the result. Reported whatever it shows. Counter visits within 30 days of the notice. Guardrail Must not get worse. Has a threshold and an action. Complaint rate; on-time renewal in each group of holders. What goes wrong. Two "primary" metrics, and the report leads with whichever improved. Two metrics are two chances of a false win.

slides.title: The minimum effect is the smallest gain that changes the decision
slides.text: Lab 1.2, step 3 The minimum effect is the smallest gain that changes the decision 0.40 riyals per holder: the reminder and the replies and complaints it brings 20 riyals: staff time to process one late renewal and its fee 2 points break-even: 0.40 / 20. Below it the reminder costs more than it saves It comes from costs and from what the director would act on, never from what the data can detect. Say points: from 61.6% to 63.6%. "2 per cent" could also mean 2% of 61.6%, which is 1.2 points.

slides.title: A guardrail has a metric, a threshold and an action
slides.text: What must not get worse A guardrail has a metric, a threshold and an action Complaint rate Threshold: the reminder arm exceeds control by more than 0.5 points. Action: stop the test and review the wording. On-time renewal in each group Groups: channel (text message, e-mail) and holder type. Threshold: a group falls more than 3 points below control. Action: stop the reminder for that group and tell the data protection officer. An average can hide a harmed group. The second guardrail is how the design applies fairness: it names the groups before anyone looks.

slides.title: The stop rule fixes the end and says what may end the test sooner
slides.text: Written before the first notice goes out The stop rule fixes the end and says what may end the test sooner The test runs 28 days and ends on the planned date. One analysis of the primary metric, at the end. One safety look on day 14 reads the guardrails only. No early stop for a good result. Who is in each arm Control: the standard notice, as today. Reminder: the same notice plus one message seven days before expiry. Nobody loses a service; the reminder is untested. What goes wrong. "We stop when the result is significant." Day 3 counts how often that rule declares a win when nothing differs.

slides.title: Which metric should carry the decision?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which metric should carry the decision? Rehab Al-Tayyar's team redesigned the online application form so that more applicants finish it. Which is the primary metric of the test? Mean time spent on each page of the form Validation errors per page view Whichever of completion, errors and time improves most The share of applicants who complete the application

slides.title: The first half of the pre-registration
slides.text: Lab 1.2 · 25 min The first half of the pre-registration Write the decision, hypothesis, primary metric, minimum effect, guardrails and stop rule of the reminder test as a record that a checklist can read. D1_2_decision_metrics.ipynb Write the decision and the hypothesis 6 min Choose the primary metric and measure its baseline 5 min Set the minimum effect from the cost table 5 min Write two guardrails with thresholds and actions 5 min Write the stop rule and run the checklist 4 min ✱ Stretch: Add a secondary metric and say why it is not a second primary metric

slides.title: Choosing the unit of randomisation
slides.text: Session 3 Choosing the unit of randomisation Choose a unit of randomisation that keeps each person in one arm Distinguish simple, stratified and cluster assignment Recognise interference between units and choose a unit that contains it 03

slides.title: The unit of randomisation is whoever the coin is tossed for
slides.text: Two units that must agree The unit of randomisation is whoever the coin is tossed for Unit of randomisation: the thing that lands in an arm as a whole: a holder, an applicant, a branch. Unit of analysis: the thing you count when you compute the result. They should be the same. When the analysis counts something smaller, the test looks larger than it is. The log tempts you Logs have one row per notice, per page view, per visit. Rows are what systems record. They are rarely what a person experiences as "getting the new version".

slides.title: One holder in five has several permits, and their notices move together
slides.text: Lab 1.3, step 1 · 20,000 past notices One holder in five has several permits, and their notices move together 20.0% of holders have several notices 38.5% of all notices go to those holders 70.7% of pairs share one outcome; 52.9% would if two notices of a holder were unrelated A coin per notice would send both versions to 60.3% of these holders. Once reminded, a holder is reminded for every permit. The unit is the holder. The test enrols each holder once, at the first notice in the window.

slides.title: 53,514 page views come from 5,068 applicants
slides.text: Lab 1.3, step 2 · the form log 53,514 page views come from 5,068 applicants Per applicant Page views Median 8 Maximum 70 Share of all rows from the busiest tenth 28.8% Among applicants with 10 or more page views, a quarter never trigger a validation error and a quarter trigger one on at least 20% of their views. A page view tells you mostly about its applicant. The unit is the applicant: one form from the first page to the last.

slides.title: Simple, stratified and cluster assignment answer different needs
slides.text: How the coin is tossed Simple, stratified and cluster assignment answer different needs Simple One coin per unit. Right when units are many and independent: 60,000 holders. Stratified Sort units into groups that matter (channel, baseline level), then toss within each group. The arms match on that trait by construction. Worth it when units are few. Cluster Toss for a whole group: a branch and everyone who visits it. Needed when people in a group affect each other. It costs power: Day 2 measures how much. Whichever you choose, the coin is seeded and recorded. Alternating days, odd and even keys chosen by hand, or "the first half of the list" are not coins.

slides.title: If one unit's treatment reaches another, the unit is too small
slides.text: When units touch each other If one unit's treatment reaches another, the unit is too small Inside a branch The counter change is a triage desk at the entrance. Visitors share one queue and one team. Sending every second visitor to the desk changes the wait of the others too. The visitor cannot be the unit. Between branches B03 and B04 share counter staff, as do B11 and B12, B19 and B20. A clerk carries the new routine next door, and staff moved to the desk are missing there. Each pair is one unit. 24 branches, 21 staff pools. The unit of the counter test is the staff pool.

slides.title: The size of a test is its number of units, not its number of rows
slides.text: Lab 1.3, step 5 The size of a test is its number of units, not its number of rows Test Rows in the log Unit Units Rows per unit Reminder 20,000 notices Holder 15,395 1.3 Form 53,514 page views Applicant 5,068 10.6 Counter 10,888 visits Staff pool 21 518.5 What goes wrong. "We have over ten thousand visits, so the test is well powered." It has 21 coin tosses.

slides.title: Whom do you toss the coin for?
slides.text: Checkpoint Whom do you toss the coin for? The office wants to test a shorter text on the ticket that the queue machine prints. All visitors of a branch wait in one hall and watch one display. What is the unit of randomisation? The branch, or the staff pool where branches share staff The visitor: each ticket printed gets a coin The day: the short text on alternate days in every branch The ticket: it is what the machine logs

slides.title: Three tests, three units
slides.text: Lab 1.3 · 25 min Three tests, three units Choose the unit for the reminder test, the form test and the counter test from evidence in the data: notices per holder, page views per applicant and branches that share staff. D1_3_three_units.ipynb Reminder test: notices per holder and how alike they are 7 min Form test: page views per applicant 5 min Counter test: branches and shared staff 6 min Record the unit of each test with its reason 4 min Count the units each test really has 3 min ✱ Stretch: If the coin were tossed per notice, what share of holders with several permits would get both versions?

slides.title: Pre-registration
slides.text: Session 4 Pre-registration Complete a one-page pre-registration with an analysis plan and planned checks State who is in each arm, why withholding is acceptable and how log data are minimised Review a pre-registration against a checklist and say what fails and why 04

slides.title: A pre-registration removes the choices you would make after seeing the data
slides.text: The reason for the page A pre-registration removes the choices you would make after seeing the data Which metric leads the report? Which holders are excluded? When does the test stop? Which subgroup is shown? Each choice is reasonable. Made after the data are in, each one leans towards the result you hoped for. Nobody has to cheat. An honest analyst who chooses late still finds too many wins. What the page is One page, dated, written before the first unit is assigned, that fixes the decision, the unit, the metrics, the size, the stop rule and the analysis. It can be amended, with a date and a reason, before the test starts. Not after.

slides.title: One page, twelve items
slides.text: The reviewer's checklist One page, twelve items C1 Decision: the action for each result C2 Hypothesis: change, metric, direction C3 Unit: nobody in both arms C4 Primary metric: exactly one, with its window C5 Minimum effect: a number with its reason C6 Guardrails: metric, threshold, action C7 Stop rule: a fixed end, no early stop for success C8 Size and duration: from the minimum effect; whole weeks and the month-end C9 Analysis plan: test, interval, unit, as assigned C10 Checks: sample ratio and balance, before the result C11 Arms and fairness: who, why withholding is acceptable, the group guardrail C12 Data: fields, pseudonymised keys, aggregate reporting

slides.title: The analysis plan is one paragraph that leaves you no choice later
slides.text: C9 The analysis plan is one paragraph that leaves you no choice later The paragraph "A two-proportion z-test and a 95% interval for the difference in on-time renewal, with holders as the unit, analysed as assigned whether or not the reminder was delivered. Subgroups by channel and by prior lateness are exploratory and are reported as such." The test and the interval are named, so they cannot be picked afterwards. The unit of analysis is the unit of randomisation. As assigned: every holder counts in the arm the coin chose. Subgroups are named now and labelled exploratory.

slides.title: Two checks are promised before anyone reads the result
slides.text: C10 Two checks are promised before anyone reads the result Sample ratio A fair coin over 60,000 holders gives about 30,000 in each arm. The page states the test and the line: a chi-square test against 50/50, failed below p = 0.001. Balance The arms should look alike on traits fixed before the test: channel, holder type, prior lateness, tenure. The page names the traits. Why promise them in advance? A check that runs only when the result disappoints is not a check. It is a search for an excuse.

slides.title: The page says which data are used and how holders stay unidentifiable
slides.text: C12 · the logs describe people The page says which data are used and how holders stay unidentifiable Question On the reminder test's page Which fields? Notice key, send date, permit type, holder type, channel, prior lateness, tenure, arm, outcomes. Nothing else. Can the analyst identify a holder? No. Keys are pseudonymised; no name, phone number or address leaves the messaging platform. How are results reported? In aggregate, never by holder; small groups are not shown. When is the extract deleted? When the report is signed. Who signs. Abdullah Al-Hogail, the data protection officer. The logs were collected to send notices; analysing them for a test is a further use, and he decides whether the page covers it.

slides.title: A script can check that a unit is written, not that it is the right one
slides.text: Lab 1.4, step 5 A script can check that a unit is written, not that it is the right one The neighbour's page states a unit: the renewal notice. The mechanical check gives it a tick. A reader fails it: a holder with three permits sits in both arms. Its "primary metric" is two metrics with the choice left open. The script sees a name and a definition. By the key, the page fails 8 of the 12 items. The rule for reviews The checklist is a list of questions for a person. Read the page, answer each question in your own words, and sign only what you could defend to the director.

slides.title: The test is running. What may still change?
slides.text: Checkpoint The test is running. What may still change? On day 10 of the reminder test the team has three ideas. Which one is compatible with the pre-registration? Make counter visits the primary metric, because they are moving more clearly End the test today, because the difference is already significant Add days until renewal as an exploratory metric, labelled as added on day 10 Drop holders whose reminder bounced from the reminder arm

slides.title: Complete and review a pre-registration
slides.text: Lab 1.4 · 25 min Complete and review a pre-registration Complete the one-page pre-registration of the reminder test from a supplied first half, run the checklist on it, then review a neighbour's page against the same checklist. D1_4_pre_registration.ipynb Load the first half; add the unit, the size and the duration 5 min Write the analysis plan and the planned checks 6 min Write the data paragraph 4 min Run the checklist on your page 3 min Review the neighbour's page against the checklist 7 min ✱ Stretch: Rewrite the neighbour's primary metric and stop rule so that they pass

slides.title: Three things to keep
slides.text: Day 1 Three things to keep The coin makes the claim Only random assignment removes what you did not measure. A volunteer comparison was wrong by 15 points in every one of 200 repetitions. The unit is who lands in an arm Holders, applicants, staff pools. 10,888 visits are 21 units. Decide before you look One primary metric, a minimum effect with a reason, guardrails with thresholds, a fixed end, an analysis plan. On one page, read by someone else.

slides.title: Is 9,200 per arm right?
slides.text: Before Day 2 Is 9,200 per arm right? Your page says 9,200 holders per arm and 28 days. Tomorrow you compute the first number, check it by simulation, and find out why the second is three times longer than the first requires. Keep your completed pre-registration at hand. Recall from DS-201: the standard error of a proportion, and what a p-value is.

slides.title: Size and run
slides.text: SDAIA Academy · Designing and Reading Experiments Size and run Day 2: How many units, for how long: the size a minimum effect demands, checked by simulation, and the calendar a test must cover Data Science Track3 teaching days + capstone day4 sessions · 4 labsDS-205

slides.title: Size and run
slides.text: Today Size and run Session 1 · Power and the minimum effect Two errors, power, the minimum effect of interest and the sample-size formula for two proportions Session 2 · Power by simulation Simulate the planned analysis many times to check power, draw a power curve and count false positives Session 3 · Cluster randomisation When whole branches are randomised: intraclass correlation, the design effect, analysis at the branch level and pairing Session 4 · Run time and seasonality Weekly cycles, the month-end peak, whole cycles and the outcome window decide how long a test runs

slides.title: Which page is ready to sign?
slides.text: Review of Day 1 Which page is ready to sign? Four pre-registrations for the reminder test differ in one line each. Which line is acceptable? Primary metric: on-time renewal or counter visits, whichever is clearer Unit: the renewal notice, since that is what the platform sends Stop rule: 28 days, one analysis at the end, a safety look at the guardrails on day 14 Guardrail: we will keep an eye on complaints

slides.title: Power and the minimum effect
slides.text: Session 1 Power and the minimum effect Explain power and the two errors a test can make Compute the sample size per arm for a minimum effect by formula Show how the minimum effect drives the size and the days of traffic needed 01

slides.title: A test can be wrong in two ways, and you choose both rates in advance
slides.text: Before any data A test can be wrong in two ways, and you choose both rates in advance The test says "effect" The test says "no clear effect" The reminder does nothing False win. You accept 5% of these: the level, α. Correct. The reminder adds 2 points Correct. The chance of landing here is the power: 80% by convention. Missed effect. 20% of the time at 80% power. Both rates are prices. A false win costs the office a reminder that does not pay. A missed effect costs it a reminder that would have.

slides.title: The same true effect gives a different estimate in every test
slides.text: Lab 2.2, step 1 The same true effect gives a different estimate in every test Simulated test Estimate p-value 1 +1.87 points 0.0086 2 +3.60 points below 0.0001 3 +1.75 points 0.0144 4 +1.90 points 0.0077 5 +0.83 points 0.2466 Five tests in one simulated world. The truth is +2 points in all five. Four find it. The fifth misses: an unlucky draw, not a wrong analysis. Power is the share of such tests that find the effect. It belongs to a design and an effect size, never to one result.

slides.title: Three things drive the sample size, and one of them is squared
slides.text: Two proportions, two arms Three things drive the sample size, and one of them is squared def n_per_arm(p1, delta, alpha=0.05, power=0.80): p2 = p1 + delta za = stats.norm.ppf(1 - alpha / 2) # 1.96 zb = stats.norm.ppf(power) # 0.84 spread = p1 * (1 - p1) + p2 * (1 - p2) return ceil((za + zb) ** 2 * spread / delta ** 2) The error rates you accept: 1.96 and 0.84. The spread of a yes-or-no outcome, largest at 50%. The minimum effect , squared, in the denominator. Only the third is open to discussion with the director.

slides.title: Two points on a baseline of 61.58% need 9,187 holders per arm
slides.text: Lab 2.1, steps 1 and 2 Two points on a baseline of 61.58% need 9,187 holders per arm 61.58% baseline on-time renewal, from 391,802 notices in 182 days 9,187 holders per arm for 2 points at 5% and 80% 18,374 holders in all: about 9 days of average traffic at 2,153 notices a day The page said 9,200. It was this calculation, rounded.

slides.title: Halve the minimum effect and the test needs four times the holders
slides.text: Lab 2.1, steps 3 and 5 Halve the minimum effect and the test needs four times the holders Minimum effect Holders per arm Against 2 points Days of average traffic 4 points 2,268 a quarter 3 2 points 9,187 1 9 1 point 36,950 four times 35 This table is the conversation with Sahar. "Would you act on 4 points only? Three days. Do you need to see 1 point? Five weeks." She chooses the row; the size follows.

slides.title: A sample size is an estimate, not a number to quote to the last holder
slides.text: Lab 2.1, step 4 and stretch A sample size is an estimate, not a number to quote to the last holder For 2 points Per arm The formula you wrote 9,187 statsmodels, same inputs 9,189 The formula at 90% power 12,298 Two honest methods differ by two holders: the library transforms the proportions first. The baseline is itself a guess about the test window. Ten more points of power cost a third more holders. Say "about 9,200 per arm".

slides.title: What does a smaller minimum effect cost?
slides.text: Checkpoint What does a smaller minimum effect cost? A test needs 6,000 residents per arm to detect 3 points. The director now says she would act on 1.5 points. About how many residents per arm does the test need? 24,000 12,000 6,000 1,500

slides.title: Sample sizes for three minimum effects
slides.text: Lab 2.1 · 25 min Sample sizes for three minimum effects Compute the sample size of the reminder test for minimum effects of 1, 2 and 4 points by formula, check it against a library and turn each size into days of traffic. D2_1_sample_sizes.ipynb Baseline rate and daily traffic from the history 4 min The formula by hand for 2 points 7 min Three minimum effects: 1, 2 and 4 points 5 min Check against a library 4 min Turn sizes into days of traffic 5 min ✱ Stretch: Repeat for 90% power and say what the extra ten points cost

slides.title: Power by simulation
slides.text: Session 2 Power by simulation Simulate a planned two-arm test and its analysis with a seed Estimate power by simulation and state its counting error Draw a power curve and read the sample size from it 02

slides.title: To check a design, run it a thousand times in a world you built
slides.text: The DS-201 habit, before the test To check a design, run it a thousand times in a world you built 1 · Build a world baseline 61.58%; the reminder truly adds 2 points → 2 · Run the plan 9,187 holders per arm, the pre-registered test → 3 · Repeat 1,000 times, with a seed → 4 · Count the share of tests that say "significant" That share is the power. If the formula is right, it should be about 80%.

slides.title: One simulated test is two binomial draws and the planned analysis
slides.text: Lab 2.2, steps 1 and 2 One simulated test is two binomial draws and the planned analysis def power_sim(gen, n, p1, delta, reps): x_c = gen.binomial(n, p1, size=reps) x_r = gen.binomial(n, p1 + delta, size=reps) _, _, p = U.z_test(x_c, n, x_r, n) return (p < 0.05).mean() power_sim(U.rng(22), 9187, 0.6158, 0.02, 1000) # 0.806 Each draw is the number of on-time renewals among n holders in one arm. The analysis is the one on the pre-registration, not a shortcut. size=reps runs all the tests at once. The seed makes your 0.806 your neighbour's 0.806.

slides.title: The simulation agrees with the formula, within its own counting error
slides.text: Lab 2.2, steps 2 and 3 The simulation agrees with the formula, within its own counting error 80% power promised by the formula at 9,187 per arm 80.6% of 1,000 simulated tests were significant ±2.5 points: two standard errors of a share counted over 1,000 tests A simulated share is an estimate too. Quote it with its error. 10,000 simulated tests would narrow the error to ±0.8 points.

slides.title: The power curve is steep at first and flat at the end
slides.text: Lab 2.2, step 4 The power curve is steep at first and flat at the end 0% 20% 40% 60% 80% 100% 0 5,000 10,000 15,000 20,000 25,000 30,000 80% power 9,187 per arm line: formula dots: 1,000 simulated tests each holders per arm Power to detect 2 points on a baseline of 61.58%. 2,000 per arm: 23.6% simulated. A real effect is missed three times in four. 9,187 per arm: 78.7% on the curve's run, 80% by formula. 30,000 per arm: every simulated test found it. The first 9,000 buy 80 points of power. The next 21,000 buy 20.

slides.title: In a world with no effect, one test in twenty still wins
slides.text: Lab 2.2, step 5 In a world with no effect, one test in twenty still wins 5.3% of 1,000 simulated tests were significant when the reminder did nothing That is the 5% you agreed to when you chose the level. It holds for one planned analysis of one metric at one moment. Tomorrow you break each of the three conditions and count again. What goes wrong. "Significant" is read as "true". At a 5% level, an office that tests twenty useless ideas adopts one of them.

slides.title: The formula covers one design; a simulation covers the one you have
slides.text: What simulation is for The formula covers one design; a simulation covers the one you have The formula assumes Independent units. Two proportions. Equal arms. One look. The baseline you guessed. Real designs break it Visitors inside branches. A baseline that turns out to be 50%: power 76.6%, not 80%. An effect that differs by weekday. An analysis on branch means. The rule. Use the formula for a first number and for the conversation about the minimum effect. Use a simulation of the planned analysis for the number you put on the page.

slides.title: What does a simulated power of 81% tell you?
slides.text: Checkpoint What does a simulated power of 81% tell you? You simulate a planned test 1,000 times with a true effect of 2 points. 81% of the simulated tests are significant. Which statement is correct? There is an 81% chance that the reminder works If the real test is significant, the effect is real with probability 81% The reminder will raise on-time renewal by 81% of 2 points If the effect is really 2 points, a test of this design finds it about 81 times in 100

slides.title: Cluster randomisation
slides.text: Session 3 Cluster randomisation Estimate the intraclass correlation and the design effect from baseline data Measure by simulation the power lost when branches are randomised in place of visitors Analyse a cluster-randomised test at the cluster level and improve it by pairing 03

slides.title: Visitors of one branch resemble each other
slides.text: The counter test Visitors of one branch resemble each other Mansour's test: a triage desk at the entrance. Outcome: served within 15 minutes. Minimum effect: 5 points. Visitors share a queue, so branches are randomised: 12 with the desk, 12 without. Four baseline weeks: 10,888 visits, 62.2% served within 15 minutes. By branch the rate runs from 43.7% to 80.3%. Intraclass correlation The share of the outcome's variance that lies between branches. Here 0.033: three per cent of the variation is about which branch you walked into.

slides.title: A small correlation times a large branch is a large penalty
slides.text: Lab 2.3, step 1 A small correlation times a large branch is a large penalty 0.033 intraclass correlation of the 15-minute outcome 454 visits per branch in four weeks, on average 15.8 design effect: 1 + (454 − 1) × 0.0326 The design effect is how many times larger the variance of the estimate is when branches are randomised in place of visitors. 10,888 visits in 24 branches carry the information of about 691 independent visits.

slides.title: Randomising branches costs 77 points of power
slides.text: Lab 2.3, steps 2 and 3 · 1,000 simulated tests each Randomising branches costs 77 points of power 100% power for 5 points if 10,888 visitors could be randomised one by one 22.8% power when 12 branches get the desk and 12 do not, analysed by branch The same visits, the same effect, the same four weeks. The test has 24 units, and branches differ from each other by far more than 5 points.

slides.title: Analysing visits from a branch-randomised test manufactures wins
slides.text: Lab 2.3, step 4 Analysing visits from a branch-randomised test manufactures wins 68.9% of tests were "significant" when the desk did nothing and visits were analysed as if each had its own coin The tempting repair: "we have 10,888 visits, use them all". The visit-level test reads the luck of which branches landed in which arm as an effect of the desk. It is not a more powerful analysis. It is a wrong one. Analyse what you randomised. One rate per branch, 24 numbers.

slides.title: Pairing like branches recovers much of the lost power
slides.text: Lab 2.3, step 5 Pairing like branches recovers much of the lost power Design Analysis Power for 5 points False wins, no effect Visitors randomised (not possible here) Visits 100% about 5% 12 and 12 branches Branch rates, t-test 22.8% 4.5% 12 and 12 branches Visits, z-test meaningless 68.9% 12 pairs of like branches Pair differences, paired t-test 62.2% 5.8% Sort branches by baseline rate, pair neighbours, toss a coin inside each pair. The stable differences between branches cancel inside the pairs.

slides.title: More branches help; more visits per branch hardly do
slides.text: When power is still short More branches help; more visits per branch hardly do More units: the strongest lever, and here there are no more branches. A longer test: helps a little; the difference between branches stays. Pairing or a baseline: removes the stable part of that difference. A larger minimum effect: an honest answer if the desk is only worth having for a large gain. And fewer units than you think Three pairs of branches share staff, so the test has 21 units, not 24. Randomised 10 against 11 without pairing, its power is 20.6%. Not on the list: a cleverer analysis of the same coin tosses.

slides.title: How large is this test?
slides.text: Checkpoint How large is this test? A ministry tests a new enrolment procedure in 16 schools, 8 with it and 8 without. Each school enrols about 600 pupils. The outcome is whether a pupil's file is complete on the first day. What decides the power of the test most? The 9,600 pupils The 16 schools and how much schools differ from each other The 600 pupils in each school The 5% significance level

Sunday to Thursday: about 2,300 notices a day. Friday and Saturday, the weekend: about 1,100 and 1,400. From the 26th: about one and a half times a normal day, because most permits fall due at the month-end.

slides.title: The cycles move the baseline rate, not only the traffic
slides.text: Lab 2.4, step 1 The cycles move the baseline rate, not only the traffic Notices sent on Mean notices a day Renewed on time Sunday to Thursday 2,360 to 2,534 62.1% to 62.6% Friday 1,203 58.3% Saturday 1,505 58.4% The 26th and later 2,974 57.6% Before the 26th 1,978 62.9% Different days, different holders. If the baseline differs by 5 points between day types, the effect of a reminder may differ too.

slides.title: The planned size is reached on day 9, a Monday
slides.text: Lab 2.4, step 2 The planned size is reached on day 9, a Monday The test starts on Sunday 6 September. A forecast gives each day its expected traffic. 18,374 holders are reached on test day 9. Stopping there, the test has seen two Sundays, two Mondays, one Friday and no month-end. What a 9-day test would estimate The effect of the reminder for holders notified in early September, with Sundays and Mondays counted twice. Nobody asked that question.

slides.title: Run whole weeks, and cover the month-end
slides.text: Lab 2.4, step 3 Run whole weeks, and cover the month-end 28 days four whole weeks from 6 September; the five month-end days fall inside 60,694 holders expected, about 30,000 per arm 1.11 points: the effect such a test detects with 80% power The calendar set the duration; the formula set only its minimum. The extra holders are not wasted: they narrow the interval around the estimate.

slides.title: A short test answers a different question
slides.text: Lab 2.4, step 4 · a planning assumption A short test answers a different question Test Holders Month-end days Expected estimate 95% margin 9 days from 6 September 18,484 0 1.86 points ±1.40 14 days from 6 September 27,682 0 1.82 points ±1.15 28 days from 6 September 60,694 5 2.35 points ±0.77 9 days from 24 September 22,430 5 3.23 points ±1.27 If the reminder adds 2 points on an ordinary day, 4 at the month-end and 1 on a weekend. Two short tests of the same reminder would report 1.9 and 3.2, and both would be called "the effect".

slides.title: Two more clocks run: the outcome window and the fading of novelty
slides.text: After the last notice Two more clocks run: the outcome window and the fading of novelty The outcome window A notice goes out 30 days before expiry. On-time renewal is known only at the expiry date. The last holders complete the metric 30 days after day 28. A result read earlier misses the holders who renew late in their window. Novelty People react to anything new, and the reaction can fade. A short test catches the reaction at its peak. A longer test averages over it and can show the effect week by week. On the page: the duration, the date on which the primary metric is complete, and a plan to report the effect by week.

slides.title: How long should this test run?
slides.text: Checkpoint How long should this test run? A test of a new payment page starts on a Sunday. The planned size is reached on day 11. Traffic is low at weekends and salaries arrive on the 27th, after which payments surge. Day 11 is the 16th of the month. What duration do you choose? 11 days 14 days 28 days As long as it takes to reach significance

slides.title: Three things to keep
slides.text: Day 2 Three things to keep The effect is squared 2 points need 9,187 per arm; 1 point needs 36,950. The minimum effect is the director's choice, made from costs. Simulate the plan 1,000 runs of the planned analysis gave 80.6% power and 5.3% false wins. When the design leaves the formula, only the simulation is left. Units and calendars 24 branches gave 22.8% power; pairing gave 62.2%. Nine days reach the size; 28 cover the weeks and the month-end.

slides.title: Which plan gives the test a fair chance?
slides.text: Review of Day 2 Which plan gives the test a fair chance? A test needs 9,000 residents per arm for its minimum effect. Traffic is 2,000 residents a day, lower at weekends, with a surge at the month-end. Which plan do you accept? Run 9 days, until 18,000 residents are in Run 28 days: whole weeks, with the month-end inside Run 9 days with 4,500 per arm to finish sooner Run until the difference is significant

slides.title: Did randomisation work
slides.text: Session 1 Did randomisation work Test whether the arm counts match the planned split Read a balance table and locate the segment in which an assignment or logging fault sits Decide which rows to analyse after a failed check and say why 01

slides.title: Check the assignment before you look at the outcome
slides.text: The order of reading Check the assignment before you look at the outcome 1 · Sample ratio are the arms the size the coin should give? → 2 · Balance do the arms look alike on traits fixed before the test? → 3 · Completeness is every assigned unit there, with its outcome? → 4 · The result only now Why this order. Once you have seen a pleasing result, every check that threatens it looks like pedantry. The page promised the checks first; keep the promise.

slides.title: 49.05% in the reminder arm is not what a fair coin gives
slides.text: Lab 3.1, step 1 · the platform's export 49.05% in the reminder arm is not what a fair coin gives 30,054 rows in the control arm of the export 28,932 rows in the reminder arm 0.000004 p-value of a chi-square test against 50/50; the page set the line at 0.001 A gap of one point looks harmless. With 59,000 rows a fair coin produces it about four times in a million. A failed check means: do not read the result until the cause is found.

slides.title: The balance table names a suspect
slides.text: Lab 3.1, step 2 The balance table names a suspect Trait fixed before the test Control Reminder p E-mail channel 15.04% 12.02% below 0.0001 Business holder 38.57% 38.34% 0.56 Late at the previous renewal 21.95% 21.96% 0.97 Tenure, years 4.63 4.60 0.17 Reading it. With four traits, one p-value near 0.05 would mean little. One that is far beyond any chance, on one trait, says where to look.

slides.title: One cell of the export is empty
slides.text: Lab 3.1, step 3 One cell of the export is empty Channel Week Control rows Reminder rows Share in the reminder arm E-mail 1 1,071 0 0.0% E-mail 2 1,017 1,075 51.4% E-mail 3 1,087 1,056 49.3% E-mail 4 1,345 1,347 50.0% Text message 1 to 4 25,534 25,454 49.9% What happened. In week 1 the reminder job failed for e-mail. The export lists a notice only when its arm's messages completed, so those holders vanished from it.

slides.title: The coin was fair. The export broke afterwards
slides.text: Lab 3.1, step 4 The coin was fair. The export broke afterwards The assignment was recorded before any message went out: 30,054 and 29,946 holders. Ratio check: p = 0.66. 1,014 holders are missing from the export. All are reminder-arm e-mail holders of week 1. They are not a typical handful: 49.6% of them renewed on time, against 63.5% of all holders. Attrition Units that drop out of one arm after assignment. When the ones that drop differ from the rest, the arms stop being comparable, and the coin's work is undone.

slides.title: The faulty export adds half a point to the reminder's credit
slides.text: Lab 3.1, step 5 The faulty export adds half a point to the reminder's credit +2.69 points: the effect computed from the export +2.17 points: the effect as assigned, on all 60,000 holders +0.53 points of bias from 1,014 missing rows What to analyse. Everyone the coin was tossed for, in the arm it chose, including the 1,014 the reminder never reached. That is "as assigned" on the page.

slides.title: A failed ratio check stops the reading, not necessarily the test
slides.text: What to do A failed ratio check stops the reading, not necessarily the test Stop reading results. Nothing computed from a broken comparison is worth quoting. Find the cell. Split by segment and by time until the loss is located. Go back to the assignment record. If it is sound and outcomes exist for everyone, analyse as assigned. If the assignment itself was faulty, or outcomes are missing for the lost units, the test cannot be repaired. Fix the cause and run it again. Write it in the result note, whichever it was.

slides.title: The ratio check has failed. What now?
slides.text: Checkpoint The ratio check has failed. What now? A form test planned a 50/50 split. The log shows 10,480 applicants on the old form and 9,720 on the new one (p below 0.0001). The new form shows a higher completion rate. What do you do first? Report the higher completion rate, with a note that the arms were unequal Delete 760 applicants at random from the old form's arm Reweight the new form's arm so that both arms count the same Find which applicants are missing from the new form's arm, and why

slides.title: Estimate, interval and effect
slides.text: Session 2 Estimate, interval and effect Compute a difference in proportions with its standard error and 95% interval Read an interval against the minimum effect and separate statistical from practical significance Report guardrails and a subgroup without overstating either 02

slides.title: The reminder raised on-time renewal by 2.17 points, give or take 0.77
slides.text: Lab 3.2, steps 1 and 2 · 60,000 holders as assigned The reminder raised on-time renewal by 2.17 points, give or take 0.77 Arm Holders Renewed on time Rate Control 30,054 18,772 62.46% Reminder 29,946 19,353 64.63% +2.17 points: the difference 0.39 points: its standard error 1.40 to 2.94 the 95% interval

slides.title: "Is there an effect?" and "Is it large enough?" are different questions
slides.text: Lab 3.2, step 3 "Is there an effect?" and "Is it large enough?" are different questions 0 +1 +2 +3 +4 no effect minimum effect: 2 points as assigned, 60,000 holders: +2.17 (1.40 to 2.94) from the faulty export: +2.69 (1.92 to 3.47) effect of the reminder on on-time renewal, points The effect as assigned, and what the faulty export would have shown. Is there an effect? Yes. Zero is far outside the interval; p is below one in a million. Is it at least 2 points? The estimate says just. The interval says: between 1.4 and 2.9. The interval straddles the minimum effect.

slides.title: An interval can sit in four places, and each has its own sentence
slides.text: The interval against the minimum effect An interval can sit in four places, and each has its own sentence Where the interval lies What to say Wholly above the minimum effect The gain is at least the minimum, beyond reasonable doubt. Above zero, straddling the minimum There is a gain. Whether it reaches the minimum is not settled. Above zero, wholly below the minimum There is a gain, and it is too small to act on. Containing zero The data are consistent with no effect, and with effects up to the upper limit. Say which. What goes wrong. All four are reported as "significant" or "not significant", which merges the first three and misdescribes the fourth.

slides.title: Guardrails are read with their intervals too
slides.text: Lab 3.2, step 4 Guardrails are read with their intervals too Guardrail or metric Effect of the reminder 95% interval Threshold Complaint rate +0.14 points up to +0.30 +0.50: held On-time renewal, e-mail holders +0.20 points −1.86 to +2.26 −3.00: held in every group On-time renewal, text-message holders +2.51 points +1.68 to +3.33 On-time renewal, business holders +1.37 points +0.11 to +2.63 On-time renewal, resident holders +2.65 points +1.68 to +3.62 Counter visits (secondary) −1.79 points −2.34 to −1.24 none "No harm found" is weaker than "harm above the threshold ruled out". Here the upper limit for complaints is below the threshold, so the stronger sentence holds.

slides.title: Compare subgroups by the interval of their difference
slides.text: Lab 3.2, step 5 · exploratory, as the page said Compare subgroups by the interval of their difference Holders Effect 95% interval Late before (13,163) +2.94 +1.23 to +4.65 Not late before (46,837) +1.94 +1.09 to +2.79 Difference +1.00 −0.91 to +2.91 The smaller subgroup has the wider interval. The difference between the two could be zero, or nearly 3 points. Report it as a hypothesis for the next test, not as a finding of this one. What goes wrong. "It works for holders who were late before." Six subgroups are six more chances of a striking number.

slides.title: The result note leads with two sentences the director can act on
slides.text: Lab 3.2, step 6 The result note leads with two sentences the director can act on The two sentences "The reminder raised on-time renewal by 2.2 points, and the data are consistent with a gain between 1.4 and 2.9 points. The estimate meets the minimum effect of 2 points, though the gain may be somewhat smaller, and no guardrail was crossed, so the evidence supports adopting the reminder." Estimate and interval first, in points. Then the reading against the minimum effect and the guardrails. Then what the pre-registered decision rule gives. The checks, the fault in the export and the subgroup follow underneath.

slides.title: How do you report this result?
slides.text: Checkpoint How do you report this result? A test of a new letter has a minimum effect of 3 points. The result: +1.2 points, 95% interval +0.4 to +2.0, p = 0.003. Which sentence is right? The letter helps, by less than the 3 points that would justify it The letter is highly effective: the result is significant at 0.003 The letter has no effect, since it missed the minimum effect The test is inconclusive and should run longer

slides.title: False wins by simulation
slides.text: Session 3 False wins by simulation Simulate A/A tests and count false wins Measure the false-win rate of peeking, of twenty metrics and of analysis at the wrong unit Apply the correct procedure to each trap and show that the rate returns to 5% 03

slides.title: In an A/A test nothing differs, so every win is false
slides.text: The measuring instrument of this session In an A/A test nothing differs, so every win is false Both arms get the same thing. The true effect is zero by construction. Run 1,000 of them and count the "significant" ones. With one planned analysis of one metric at the right unit: 5.5% of 1,000. That is the 5% you agreed to. Anything above it was added by a habit. Three habits, three counts Looking every day. Looking at twenty metrics. Counting page views in place of applicants. Each feels harmless, and each can be found in reports written by careful people.

slides.title: A p-value wanders, and 28 looks give it 28 chances to cross 0.05
slides.text: Lab 3.3, step 2 A p-value wanders, and 28 looks give it 28 chances to cross 0.05 0.01 0.05 0.2 1 day 1 day 7 day 14 day 21 day 28 0.05 test day (no true effect in any of the three tests) Three A/A tests that dipped below 0.05 and came back. Rule: stop on the first day the p-value is below 0.05. 27.8% of 1,000 A/A tests declare a win. Half of those false wins are declared by day 5.

slides.title: One analysis at the planned end restores the 5%
slides.text: The correct procedure, in this course One analysis at the planned end restores the 5% 27.8% false wins: 28 daily looks, stop at the first p below 0.05 14.5% false wins: four weekly looks 5.5% false wins: one look, on day 28 A test stopped early on a false win also reports a large "effect": only large swings cross the line with little data. Planned interim looks are possible with methods that spend the 5% across the looks. They are the subject of DS-302.

slides.title: With twenty metrics, most tests of nothing show a "significant" one
slides.text: Lab 3.3, step 3 With twenty metrics, most tests of nothing show a "significant" one 64.1% of A/A tests have at least one of twenty metrics below 0.05 5.5% after Holm's correction for twenty 5.5% with one pre-registered primary metric The chance that none of twenty unrelated metrics crosses is 0.95 to the power 20: 36%. Two honest ways out: one primary metric named in advance, or a correction for the number examined. Subgroups count the same way.

slides.title: Counting page views for applicants turns luck into significance
slides.text: Lab 3.3, step 4 · the form log, with applicants dealt a fresh coin Counting page views for applicants turns luck into significance 34.0% of A/A tests are significant when 53,514 page views are analysed as independent 5.8% when the 5,068 applicants are analysed, as randomised The page-level test believes it has ten times the information it has, so its standard error is too small. Ordinary luck in which struggling applicants landed where then looks like an effect.

slides.title: Each habit multiplies the false-win rate; each correct procedure restores it
slides.text: Lab 3.3, step 5 Each habit multiplies the false-win rate; each correct procedure restores it Trap False wins with the trap With the correct procedure Peeking: 28 daily looks, stop at the first p below 0.05 27.8% 5.5% (one look at the planned end) Many metrics: any of twenty 64.1% 5.5% (Holm, or one primary metric) Wrong unit: page views for applicants 34.0% 5.8% (analyse applicants) They combine. A report that peeked at many metrics per page view is close to a machine for producing wins. None of the three needs a wrong formula.

slides.title: Novelty fades and attrition unbalances, even when the analysis is right
slides.text: Two traps that no A/A test shows Novelty fades and attrition unbalances, even when the analysis is right Novelty A first-week reaction to anything new, which can fade. A test of eight days measures the reaction at its peak. Look for the effect by week, and distrust short tests of visible changes. Attrition Units that drop out of one arm after assignment: a reminder that never arrived, a form that crashed on some devices. The remaining arms differ in who is left. Look at the sample ratio and at who is missing. Both change the true comparison, not the false-win rate. They are found by reading the design and the checks, which is the next session.

slides.title: Which habit produced this win?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which habit produced this win? A team planned a 4-week test of a new queue screen in 30 branches with one primary metric. They analysed it once, at the end, and report: "average wait fell, p = 0.01, n = 41,000 visits". Which trap should you check first? Peeking Many metrics Wrong unit of analysis Novelty

D3_3_false_wins.ipynb One look at the end: the 5% you agreed to 4 min Peeking: a look every day for 28 days 7 min Twenty metrics: any win, then a correction 6 min Wrong unit: page views against applicants 5 min The table of false-win rates 3 min ✱ Stretch: Peek once a week only, four looks: how much of the damage remains?

slides.title: Reviewing a reported result
slides.text: Session 4 Reviewing a reported result Review a write-up in a fixed order: design, checks, analysis, claim Name each flaw with its consequence for the reported result State the decision the evidence does support and defend it 04

slides.title: Review in a fixed order: design, checks, analysis, claim
slides.text: Reading someone else's result Review in a fixed order: design, checks, analysis, claim 1 · Design what did the page promise: unit, primary metric, size, stop rule? → 2 · Checks did the arms survive: ratio, balance, missing units? → 3 · Analysis was the promised analysis run, at the unit that was randomised, once? → 4 · Claim does the recommendation follow, for the units and the period tested? Read the result last. A reviewer who starts with the headline spends the rest of the page defending or attacking it.

slides.title: "The redesigned form works. Roll it out to every form."
slides.text: Lab 3.4 · the form redesign test "The redesigned form works. Roll it out to every form." What was planned Primary metric: the share of applicants who complete the application. Minimum effect: 3 points. Unit: the applicant. A run of 28 days with one analysis at the end. What the write-up reports "We watched the dashboard every morning. On day 8 the difference in validation errors was clearly significant, so we stopped." Errors per page view fell from 13.0% to 12.0%, "highly significant" with 53,514 page views. Completion 58.5% against 59.3%, p = 0.54. "We examined 14 metrics." "The redesigned form logged fewer applicants. We put this down to chance."

slides.title: Seven flaws, each with a place in the text
slides.text: Lab 3.4, step 1 Seven flaws, each with a place in the text Flaw Where in the write-up Metric switch The headline is errors per page view; the page promised completion Wrong unit A z-test on page views; applicants were randomised Peeking Watched every morning, stopped on a significant day Ratio mismatch and attrition 2,738 against 2,330 applicants, "put down to chance" Many comparisons 14 metrics, and the strongest subgroup Short run 8 days of a planned 28: one weekend, no month-end Overclaim "Proven"; all forms; 9,000 more applications a year And three it does not have: a control arm exists, a seeded coin assigned, both arms were measured alike. A review that cries wolf loses its reader.

slides.title: A review that only reads is an opinion: recompute
slides.text: Lab 3.4, step 2 A review that only reads is an opinion: recompute "We put this down to chance" 2,738 against 2,330 applicants: ratio check p = 0.00000001. By device: 379 applicants on old mobile browsers in the current arm, none in the redesigned arm. "Highly significant with 53,514 page views" Per page view: 13.0% against 12.0%, p = 0.0002. Per applicant, as randomised: 13.0% against 12.3%, p = 0.25. Two lines of code each. The log was available to the author too.

slides.title: The memo goes from each flaw to its consequence to a decision
slides.text: Lab 3.4, step 3 The memo goes from each flaw to its consequence to a decision 1 · Flaw and consequence Not "the unit is wrong" but "counted per applicant, the difference in errors is not significant". 2 · What the evidence supports "The test does not support a roll-out. It shows no reliable difference in completion, and a redesign that fails on old mobile browsers." 3 · The next step "Fix the browser fault. Run the full 28 days as pre-registered, one analysis, completion as primary, applicants as the unit, ratio check first." What goes wrong. A memo that ends at "the analysis is flawed" leaves the director with a decision and nothing to make it with.

slides.title: The test did find something, and the write-up put it down to chance
slides.text: Lab 3.4, steps 2 and stretch The test did find something, and the write-up put it down to chance The redesigned form does not work on old mobile browsers. 379 of them used the current form in eight days; a roll-out would turn away about twice that. On devices logged in both arms, completion is 61.0% on the current form and 59.3% on the redesign: the "right direction" disappears. That second comparison is a repair made after the fact. It shows how fragile the claim is; it does not prove the reverse. A reviewer's best contribution Not the list of errors. The thing the data were saying that the author did not want to hear.

slides.title: Which decision does the evidence support?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which decision does the evidence support? A write-up reports a randomised test of a new appointment text, analysed as pre-registered: missed appointments fell by 1.9 points (0.4 to 3.4), against a minimum effect of 1.5. It then recommends the text "for all clinics, and for vaccination reminders too". The test ran in the city's eight clinics. What do you write? Reject the write-up: the claim goes beyond the evidence Adopt the text for appointments in the eight clinics; test vaccination reminders separately Accept the recommendation as written: the test was sound Ask for a longer test before deciding anything

slides.title: Review a write-up
slides.text: Lab 3.4 · 25 min Review a write-up Find the seeded flaws in the write-up of the form test, recompute two of its claims from the log, draft the review memo and choose a capstone case. D3_4_review_memo.ipynb Read the write-up and mark the flaws 7 min Recompute two claims from the log 7 min Draft the memo: flaw, consequence, supported decision 8 min Choose your capstone case 3 min ✱ Stretch: Compare completion only on devices that were logged in both arms

slides.title: Three things to keep
slides.text: Day 3 Three things to keep Checks before results A ratio of 49.05% hid 1,014 missing holders and half a point of bias. Analyse everyone as assigned. Intervals over verdicts +2.17 points, 1.40 to 2.94, against a minimum of 2. Say what is settled and what is not. Wins are cheap Peeking 27.8%, twenty metrics 64.1%, page views 34.0%. One look, one metric, the right unit: about 5%.

slides.title: One case, the whole course
slides.text: Before the capstone day One case, the whole course Your pack: a pre-registration, a sample-size notebook with a power curve, an analysis notebook, a result note and a review memo, in a public repository. Start with the pre-registration, and commit it before you open the experiment log. You may use an assistant for the work. You defend it without one. Rehearse the question you will be asked: "the minimum effect is now half; what is the size?"

slides.title: How the defences run
slides.text: Capstone How the defences run Expectations and final prep the rubric, a last rerun of the notebooks, then the first defences Defences eight minutes on one design choice, then four minutes of questions Review and closing peer feedback, the trainer's review, the follow-up task

slides.title: The rubric
slides.text: How the pack and its defence are scored The rubric Design and pre-registration 25% Power and sample size 25% Analysis and checks 20% Review memo 20% Writing and reproducibility 10% Every number in the notes comes out of a seeded rerun. The pre-registration is committed before the experiment log is opened.

slides.title: 8 minutes for the defence, then 4 minutes of questions
slides.text: Format 8 minutes for the defence, then 4 minutes of questions 1 · The decision The case, the decision in one sentence with its number, and the unit you randomise with the reason. 2 · One design choice The unit, the size or the duration: what you chose, the evidence from your notebooks, and a live rerun with the seed. 3 · The reading Checks first, then the estimate with its interval against the minimum effect, and what the write-up got wrong. In the questions, the assessor changes the minimum effect or the unit. You say what happens to the size and the duration, then recompute and show it.

slides.title: Three cases, one pack each
slides.text: The cases Three cases, one pack each Case Minimum effect What makes it hard A A reminder message for the annual stall inspection 3 points of booking within 14 days A guardrail that needs its interval B A redesigned form for building-works permits 3 points of completion A sound result inside a poor write-up C A training programme for counter staff in 20 service centres 4 points of first-visit resolution Clusters, and a first wave that was not randomised All data are synthetic and seeded. Each case has a history file, a completed experiment log and a write-up to review.
